cluster: origen-own: Origen in his own words (On First Principles and the works that survive in Greek)
summary: Origen's own words can be set beside the later quarrels, but nearly everything in his central book, On First Principles, survives only in Rufinus's Latin, and Rufinus says he smoothed passages he believed heretics had corrupted. Read in that Latin, the Preface lists what the church's preaching has settled (eternal fire is on the settled list) and what it leaves open (where the soul comes from, what the devil and angels are, what came before and will come after this world). Chapter 1.6.1-2 offers the idea that the end is like the beginning as inquiry rather than definition; 2.10.4-6 pictures punishment as a physician's fire that mends a dissolved soul; and 3.6 describes a restoration that comes in stages, with the body changed rather than destroyed. Against Celsus, which survives in Greek, says in 6.26 that the full account of punishment is not for the many, and in 8.72 that the Word will one day master every rational soul and abolish evil, while declining to say whether evil could ever return. Homilies on Jeremiah 20 (also Greek) defends a God who ‘deceives’ for good and speaks of a ‘mystery’ the many must not learn, but the lines read never say what the hidden truth about punishment is. The Commentary on Romans (Rufinus's abridged Latin) says in 5.10 that Christ's cross suffices for past, present and future ages and that love, which never fails, will keep the whole creation from falling, and in 6.5 that ‘eternal’ can mean a lifetime or this present age, though eternal life with the Lord has no end. Where Rufinus and the hostile Greek in Justinian's Letter to Menas (543) differ, as at 1.2.13, editors split: Koetschau (and so Butterworth, who translated his text) trust the Greek and print a mixed text, while Crouzel-Simonetti and Behr print Rufinus and move the Greek aside. Scholars read the lines along familiar lines: Ramelli and Hannen find a consistent universal restoration, Crouzel calls it a hope that cannot be certain without denying freedom, and McClymond, Heide and Batiffol stress the hedges, the care about audience and the limits. Caution on method: the Latin of On First Principles and of the Romans commentary below is Migne's (Patrologia Graeca 11 and 14, Delarue's text) read from OCR page transcriptions, not Koetschau's or Hammond Bammel's critical text, which could not be reached.

passages.title: The rule of faith, and what the church's preaching leaves open (On First Principles, Preface 4-10)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles (Peri Archon, De principiis), Preface 4-10, in Rufinus's Latin translation
passages.date: Origen's Greek: written in Alexandria, before c. 230 (exact date disputed). Rufinus's Latin: 397-98.
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; the Greek of the Preface is lost)
passages.original: (4) Species vero eorum quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo quod unus Deus est qui omnia creavit atque composuit … Tum deinde honore ac dignitate Patri ac Filio sociatum tradiderunt Spiritum sanctum. In hoc non jam manifeste discernitur, utrum natus an innatus vel Filius etiam Dei ipse habendus sit, necne. Sed inquirenda jam ista pro viribus sunt de sacra Scriptura, et sagaci perquisitione investiganda. (5) Post haec jam quod anima substantiam vitamque habens propriam, cum ex hoc mundo discesserit, pro suis meritis dispensabitur, sive vitae aeternae ac beatitudinis haereditate potitura, si hoc ei sua gesta praestiterint; sive igni aeterno ac suppliciis mancipanda … Est et illud definitum in ecclesiastica praedicatione, omnem animam rationabilem esse liberi arbitrii et voluntatis … De anima vero utrum ex seminis traduce ducatur, ita ut ratio ipsius vel substantia inserta ipsis seminibus corporalibus habeatur, an vero aliud habeat initium: et hoc ipsum initium si genitum est, aut non genitum: vel certe si extrinsecus corpori inditur, necne: non satis manifesta praedicatione distinguitur. (6) De diabolo et angelis ejus contrariisque virtutibus ecclesiastica praedicatio docuit, quoniam sunt quidem haec; quae autem sint, aut quomodo sint, non satis clare exposuit. (7) … Quid tamen ante hunc mundum fuerit, aut quid post mundum erit, jam non pro manifesto multis innotuit. (10) … De sole autem et luna et stellis utrum animantia sint, an sine anima, manifeste non traditur.
passages.edition: Standard critical edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke 5: De principiis (Peri archon), Griechische christliche Schriftsteller (GCS) 22 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1913), Praefatio 4-10; page not confirmed. Modern editions with translation: H. Crouzel and M. Simonetti, Origene: Traite des principes, Sources Chretiennes (SC) 252 (Paris: Cerf, 1978); J. Behr, Origen: On First Principles, Oxford Early Christian Texts (Oxford: OUP, 2017). Neither was opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau (the archive.org scan of GCS 22 could not be read in sections; see problems). Checked against the Latin of Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11 (Paris, 1857; Delarue's text), cols. 117-122, from OCR page transcriptions: Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica (teste/PG011, second batch, pages 063-064) and OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11 (hvd.32044024345175_ocr, page 066), compared with two further OCR copies of the same page for section 4. The ligatures ae and oe are written out. The spelling (j, haereditas) is Migne's, not Koetschau's. One clause in section 5 (‘si in hoc eam scelerum culpa … ’) was left out because the OCR gave a doubtful verb.
passages.english: (4) The main points of what is plainly handed down through the apostles' preaching are these. First, that there is one God, who created and arranged all things … Then they handed down that the Holy Spirit is joined with the Father and the Son in honour and dignity. About this it is not yet clearly distinguished whether he is born or unborn, or whether he is also to be counted a Son of God, or not. But these matters must be inquired into, as far as we are able, from the sacred Scripture, and tracked down by a keen search. (5) Next, that the soul, having its own substance and life, when it leaves this world will be dealt with according to its merits: either to inherit eternal life and blessedness, if its deeds have earned it, or to be handed over to eternal fire and punishments … It is also settled in the church's preaching that every rational soul has free choice and will … But as to the soul, whether it is passed on by descent, so that its principle or substance is contained in the bodily seeds themselves, or whether it has some other beginning, and whether that beginning is itself begotten or unbegotten, or again whether it is put into the body from outside or not: this is not distinguished with sufficient clarity in the preaching. (6) About the devil and his angels and the opposing powers, the church's preaching has taught that they exist; what they are or how they exist it has not set out clearly enough. (7) … But what there was before this world, or what will be after the world, has not yet become plain to many. (10) … As to the sun, moon and stars, whether they are living beings or without soul, nothing is plainly handed down.
passages.english_source: Own translation. For comparison: F. Crombie in the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (1885, public domain); G. W. Butterworth (1936); J. Behr (2017). None was opened for this entry. Contested renderings: ‘aeternus’ (eternal or age-long) in ‘igni aeterno’ and ‘vita aeterna’; ‘natus an innatus’ (born/unborn, or begotten/unbegotten, or made/unmade, see the note); ‘praedicatio ecclesiastica’ (the church's preaching, proclamation or teaching).
passages.why_it_matters: This is Origen's own list of what the church's preaching has settled and what it has not. Eternal fire is on the settled list; the origin of the soul, the nature of the devil and angels, and the time before and after this world are not. Later condemnations (the 553 anathemas) treat some of those open questions, pre-existence above all, as heresy, so the argument is over whether Origen offered them as inquiry or taught them as doctrine.
passages.textual_notes: Migne's apparatus (cols. 117-120) records the manuscript readings Delarue preferred over the earlier printed editions. The most telling is note 51: where Rufinus has ‘natus an innatus’ (begotten or unbegotten) for the Spirit, Jerome's Letter 94 (= 124) to Avitus renders it ‘factus an infectus’ (made or unmade); Delarue reasons that Jerome read the Greek with one nu (genetos/agenetos, created/uncreated) and Rufinus with two (gennetos/agennetos, begotten/unbegotten). That one-letter difference decides whether Origen is asking if the Spirit is a creature. Note 55: the manuscripts read ‘extrinsecus corpori inditur’ (put in from outside) where some earlier editions had ‘intrinsecus’. Notes 53-54: a clause of section 5 is also found in the Apology for Origen by Pamphilus (in Rufinus's Latin), which is one of the few controls on Rufinus. Rufinus's own preface (Jerome Letter 80) says he removed or corrected passages he thought heretics had inserted; the c400 file in this survey has that text. Section numbers follow Migne/Delarue; they agree with Koetschau's in the Preface as far as I could tell, not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Michael McClymond
readings.work: ‘Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus: A Review of Ilaria Ramelli's The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis’, Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), pp. 815, 818-19
readings.position: Reports that the speculations in On First Principles (pre-existent souls, the resurrected body, the reconciliation of Satan and the demons, multiple lives, universal salvation) drew the charge of ‘dogmatizing’, and that Rufinus's claim that heretics had corrupted the text left later readers with a skewed Latin version. The part of the review I could read does not show whether he thinks the charge was fair.
readings.side: notes that Origen was accused of treating open questions as doctrine; presses the Rufinus problem against Ramelli's defence

readings.scholar: Mark Edwards and Panayiotis Tzamalikos (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Edwards, Origen against Plato (2002); Tzamalikos, Origen: Philosophy of History and Eschatology (Brill, 2007); reported in Martens's review of Mark Scott, Journey Back to God, in Marginalia, and in this survey's REPORT.md
readings.position: Both deny that Origen taught the pre-existence of souls at all. Martens faults Scott for treating pre-existence as Origen's without an extended answer to them. The reports I saw do not tie their argument to the Preface by name.
readings.side: Origen did not teach pre-existence, so what the 553 text condemns is not his doctrine

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 124 to Avitus, 124.4.5 (Hilberg, CSEL 56, c. 100); Latin text as given in this survey's c400 file
readings.position: Quotes Origen's own plea that the speculations are ‘not dogmas but only questions raised and thrown out’, the disclaimer the Preface and 1.6.1 announce, while attacking the content of the book. How he uses it is set out in the c400 file.
readings.side: ancient hostile reader who reports the disclaimer and judges the doctrine anyway

passages.title: ‘The end is always like the beginning’ (On First Principles 1.6.1-2)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 1.6.1-2 (Rufinus's Latin); the sentence is cited as 1.6.2
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; no Greek survives for these lines)
passages.original: (1.6.1) … Quae quidem a nobis etiam cum magno metu et cautela dicuntur, discutientibus magis et pertractantibus quam pro certo ac definito statuentibus. … Nunc autem disputandi specie magis quam definiendi, prout possumus, exercemur. … In unum sane finem putamus quod bonitas Dei per Christum suum universam revocet creaturam, subactis et subditis etiam inimicis. (1.6.2) Talem igitur finem videntes, cum omnes inimici subjecti erunt Christo, et cum novissimus inimicus destruetur mors, et cum tradetur a Christo cui omnia subjecta sunt, regnum Deo Patri, ab isto, inquam, tali fine rerum contemplemur initia. Semper enim similis est finis initiis; et ideo sicut unus omnium finis, ita unum omnium intelligi debet initium; et sicut multorum unus finis, ita ab uno initio multae differentiae ac varietates, quae rursum per bonitatem Dei et subjectionem Christi, atque unitatem Spiritus sancti in unum finem qui sit initio similis revocantur.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913); Hilberg's source notes (as quoted in the c400 file) put 1.6.2-3 at pp. 81-83, which I did not check myself. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978); Behr (OUP, 2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 165-166 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, first batch, page 087), which separates the main text from Delarue's notes. Ligatures written out; no other change.
passages.english: (1.6.1) … We say these things with great fear and caution, discussing and weighing them rather than laying them down as certain and defined. … Here, as well as we can, we are exercising ourselves in the manner of a debate rather than of a definition. … We think that the goodness of God, through his Christ, will call back his whole creation into one end, with even the enemies conquered and subdued. (1.6.2) Seeing such an end, when all enemies shall be subject to Christ, when the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed, and when the kingdom is handed over by Christ, to whom all things are subject, to God the Father: from that end, I say, let us consider the beginnings. For the end is always like the beginnings; and therefore, as we must understand one end of all things, so also one beginning of all; and as there is one end of many, so from one beginning come many differences and varieties, which are in turn called back, through God's goodness, the subjection of Christ and the unity of the Holy Spirit, into one end that is like the beginning.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘finis’ (end, goal or purpose); ‘revocet’ and ‘revocantur’ (call back, recall, restore; the Greek verb behind them is not preserved); ‘putamus’ (we think, i.e. a hedged claim); ‘initiis’ is plural (beginnings); ‘universam creaturam’ (the whole creation, which may or may not include the devil and demons: Rufinus and Jerome disagree).
passages.why_it_matters: These lines are the source of the famous sentence that the end is like the beginning, which the 553 fifteen anathemas echo (‘the end and the beginning shall be alike’). The argument is over what ‘beginning’ means (a state of bodiless pre-existent minds, or only God's original purpose) and how firmly the surrounding words claim it: Origen frames it as discussion ‘rather than definition’.
passages.textual_notes: Delarue marks the key sentences ‘Cautè lege’ (read with caution) in notes 57, 58, 60, 61 and 64 and, in note 62, says that Jerome (Letter 94 = 124 to Avitus) attacks this very place. Note 51: some earlier editions had ‘videtur esse judicium’ where the manuscripts have ‘videtur indicium’ (a sign). Note 54: the manuscripts read ‘fidem ecclesiasticam’ where earlier editions had ‘catholicam’. The word ‘putamus’ (we think) in ‘In unum sane finem putamus’ is Rufinus's; if his Greek had a stronger verb, this is where he could have softened it, which is the kind of question the c400 file raises about 1.6.3.

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 94 (also numbered 124) to Avitus, quoted in Delarue's note 62 at PG 11 col. 166
readings.position: Reads 1.6.2 as teaching an endless cycle: ‘the beginning is born again from the end and the end from the beginning; and so all things change, so that he who is now a man could become a demon in another world; and a demon who has acted rather carelessly is banished into coarser bodies, that is, becomes a man. So he mixes everything up, so that from an angel the devil can come to be and the devil return to being an angel.’ (Own translation of the Latin as printed in the note.)
readings.side: ancient hostile reader: takes ‘end like beginning’ to mean endless cycling between angel, man and devil

readings.scholar: Michael McClymond
readings.work: ‘Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus’, Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), p. 824 n. 24
readings.position: Quotes ‘the end is always like the beginning’ to show that Origen's apokatastasis (restoration of all things) is a return to a state that existed before, and contrasts this with Gregory of Nyssa's rejection of pre-existent souls. His wider charge is that Ramelli does not keep Origen apart from Gregory of Nyssa.
readings.side: reads the sentence as tied to Origen's pre-existence, so not a model for Nyssa's universalism

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), pp. 197-199 incl. n. 13
readings.position: Reads chapter 1.6 as saying God's goodness through Christ will restore all creation to one end, with punishments as methods of correction rather than eternal retribution, while Origen hedges on whether the devil's redemption is settled; cites Jennifer Heckart (Union Seminary Quarterly Review 60) for his denial of teaching it.
readings.side: reads 1.6 as teaching restoration of creation with the devil's case left open

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen: The Eschatological Conception of Apokatastasis’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 24, citing Crouzel
readings.position: Treats On First Principles as ‘research theology’: Origen speaks of the end with caution, ‘in the manner rather of an investigation and discussion’, not as a fixed decision.
readings.side: reads 1.6 as inquiry that does not claim to define

passages.title: Punishment as a physician's fire (On First Principles 2.10.4-6)
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's translation; no Greek survives for these sections)
passages.original: (2.10.4) … ita anima cum multitudinem malorum operum et abundantiam in se congregaverit peccatorum, competenti tempore omnis illa malorum congregatio effervescit ad supplicium, atque inflammatur ad poenas; … tunc et ipsa conscientia propriis stimulis agitatur atque compungitur, et sui ipsa efficitur accusatrix et testis. … (2.10.5) … Quae animae dissolutio atque divulsio cum adhibiti ignis ratione fuerit explorata, sine dubio ad firmiorem sui compaginem instaurationemque solidatur. (2.10.6) Multa sunt etiam alia quae nos latent, quae illi soli cognita sunt, qui est medicus animarum nostrarum. … quanto magis intelligendum est et hunc medicum nostrum Deum volentem diluere vitia animarum nostrarum, quae ex peccatorum et scelerum diversitate collegerant, ut huiuscemodi poenalibus curis, insuper etiam ignis inferre supplicium his qui sanitatem animae perdiderunt? … Ex quo utique intelligitur quod furor vindictae Dei ad purgationem proficit animarum. Quoniam autem et ea poena quae per ignem inferri dicitur, pro adjutorio intelligitur adhiberi, Isaias docet …
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), Book 2 chapter 10; page not confirmed. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978), where Sytsma places 2.10.8 at pp. 392-394; Behr (2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 237-240 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, first batch, pages 122-124). The wording ‘ut huiuscemodi poenalibus curis, insuper etiam ignis inferre supplicium’ is copied as the scan has it; the construction is awkward and the Latin may differ in Koetschau (ignis for igni?). Ligatures written out.
passages.english: (2.10.4) … So when the soul has gathered into itself a great mass of evil deeds and an abundance of sins, at the fitting time that whole accumulation of evils boils up into punishment and is set on fire for penalties; … then the conscience itself is stirred and pricked by its own goads and becomes its own accuser and witness. … (2.10.5) … When this dissolution and tearing apart of the soul has been tested by the working of the fire applied to it, it is without doubt rebuilt into a firmer structure and made whole. (2.10.6) There are many other things that escape us, known only to him who is the physician of our souls. … How much more must we understand that this physician of ours, God, wishing to wash out the vices of our souls, which they had gathered from the variety of sins and crimes, applies to such cures the further punishment of fire for those who have lost the soul's health? … From this it is understood that the fury of God's vengeance serves the purging of souls. And that the punishment said to be brought by fire is understood to be applied as a help, Isaiah teaches …
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘furor vindictae’ (fury or anger of vengeance; the Latin may reflect Greek orge); ‘purgationem’ (purging or purification); ‘ignem’ is the fire of punishment but Origen treats it as the soul's own passions in 2.10.4-5, so ‘fire’ is partly figurative.
passages.why_it_matters: Here Origen most clearly describes punishment after death as medicine: the fire is the soul's own inflamed sins, and God uses it to rebuild what has come apart. Whether that means punishment ends (and so restoration) is the question the sixth-century anathema on ‘temporary punishment’ answers with a condemnation; Origen himself in these sections does not say how long it lasts.
passages.textual_notes: Adjacent and disputed: at 2.10.8 Koetschau supplied, from Jerome and Justinian, a sentence he thought Rufinus had omitted: ‘There is a resurrection of the dead, and there is punishment, but not everlasting’ (reported by Sytsma, p. 11 n. 23, citing Butterworth p. 146 and SC 252 pp. 392-394). Sections 4-6 are Rufinus's Latin without a Greek control. Delarue's section numbers are used here; Koetschau's numbering agrees as far as I can tell, not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), pp. 25-26
readings.position: Reads 2.10 as teaching that punishment is remedial, like a physician's treatment, a limited process leading to restoration, demons included; quotes ‘for all wicked men, and for demons, too, punishment has an end’ (from the 2.10 material) and notes that Origen contradicts himself on Satan's salvation, citing Holliday and Heckart (nn. 60-61).
readings.side: reads 2.10 as teaching limited, curative punishment ending in restoration

readings.scholar: Paul Koetschau (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), p. 11 n. 23, on Koetschau's text of 2.10.8
readings.position: Koetschau believed Rufinus left out at 2.10.8 the sentence ‘There is a resurrection of the dead, and there is punishment, but not everlasting’, and restored it from the hostile Greek and Jerome.
readings.side: treats Rufinus as having softened the passage on the end of punishment

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as cited by Daniel Heide)
readings.work: Crouzel, ‘L'Hades et la Geheenne selon Origene’ (1978), cited in Heide, Dionysius 33 (2015), n. 28
readings.position: Heide cites Crouzel's study of Origen on Hades and Gehenna for Origen's ambiguity about whether and when punishment ends. The report does not give Crouzel's own wording or tie it to 2.10.4-6 by section.
readings.side: reads Origen on the duration of punishment as ambiguous

passages.title: God ‘all in all’: restoration in stages, and the body changed, not destroyed (On First Principles 3.6)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 3.6.1, 3.6.3 and 3.6.6 (Rufinus's Latin), with a Greek fragment at 3.6.3 preserved by Justinian
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus's Latin 397-98
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus), with one Greek fragment (Justinian's Letter to Menas, 543)
passages.original: (3.6.1) … Igitur summum bonum ad quod natura rationabilis universa festinat, quod etiam finis omnium dicitur, a quamplurimis etiam philosophorum hoc modo terminatur, quia summum bonum sit, prout possibile est, similem fieri Deo. … (3.6.3) … quod non solum in omnibus esse dicitur Deus, sed etiam omnia in omnibus. Quae sint ergo ista omnia quae Deus futurus sit in omnibus, requiramus. … (3.6.6) … cum sensim et per singulos emendatio fuerit et correctio prosecuta, praecurrentibus aliis et velociori cursu ad summa tendentibus, aliis vero proximo quoque spatio insequentibus, tum deinde aliis longe posterius, et sic per multos et innumeros ordines proficientium ac Deo se ex inimicis reconciliantium pervenitur usque ad novissimum inimicum qui dicitur mors, ut etiam ipse destruatur ne ultra sit inimicus. Cum ergo restitutae fuerint omnes rationabiles animae in huiuscemodi statum, tunc natura etiam huius corporis nostri in spiritalis corporis gloriam perducetur. … non aliud corpus est quo nunc in ignobilitate et in corruptione et infirmitate utimur, et aliud erit illud quo in incorruptione, et in virtute, et in gloria utemur; sed hoc idem abjectis his infirmitatibus in quibus nunc est, in gloriam transmutabitur spiritale effectum, ut quod fuit indignitatis vas, hoc ipsum expurgatum fiat vas honoris et beatitudinis habitaculum.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), Book 3 chapter 6; page not confirmed. Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 268 (1980; volume number from memory); Behr (OUP, 2017): not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Koetschau. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 333-340 (Delarue's text), from OCR page transcriptions in OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11: mdp.39015013266690_ocr pages 180, 181, 183 and hvd.32044024345175_ocr pages 172, 175. Two-column pages were read in several copies and only contiguous lines are quoted. The OCR drops large parts of some pages, so section 3.6.5 (the passage on the destruction of the last enemy, which I recall says that what is destroyed is the enemy's will, not its substance) was NOT obtained; 3.6.6 is quoted instead for the same point. Ligatures written out; ‘restitutae’ and ‘abjectis’ corrected from OCR slips (‘restitutte’, ‘abjectis’ already as printed).
passages.english: (3.6.1) … The highest good, toward which all rational nature hurries, which is also called the end of all things, is defined by very many of the philosophers too in this way: that the highest good is to become like God, as far as is possible. … (3.6.3) … that God is said to be not only in all things but also all things in all. Let us ask, then, what those ‘all things’ are that God will be in all. … (3.6.6) … when, little by little and one by one, amendment and correction have gone forward — some running ahead and reaching the heights at a swifter pace, others following close behind, others again much later — and so through many and countless ranks of those advancing and being reconciled to God from being enemies, one comes at last to the last enemy, which is called death, so that even he is destroyed and is no longer an enemy. When, then, all rational souls have been restored to such a state, then the nature of this body of ours too will be carried up into the glory of the spiritual body. … It is not one body that we now use in dishonour, corruption and weakness, and another that we shall use in incorruption, power and glory; rather this same body, its present weaknesses cast off, will be changed into glory, made spiritual, so that what was a vessel of dishonour, once purified, becomes a vessel of honour and a dwelling of blessedness.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Crombie (ANF 4, 1885, public domain); Butterworth (1936); Behr (2017), none opened. Contested renderings: ‘restitutae’ (restored; the Greek is apokatastasis-language, so ‘restoration’ and ‘universal salvation’ are the two usual glosses); ‘destruatur’ (destroyed, abolished or put out of action: the point is whether the enemy ceases to exist or ceases to be an enemy); ‘Deus omnia in omnibus’ (1 Cor 15:28: God all in all, or God everything in everyone); ‘rationabiles animae’ (rational souls or rational beings).
passages.why_it_matters: This chapter is Origen's fullest account of the end. Three points are in dispute between readers: whether ‘all in all’ includes the wicked and the devil, whether the stages of amendment end with every rational being restored, and whether the body is abolished (the Greek fragment below, and Justinian's use of it) or only transformed (Rufinus's Latin).
passages.textual_notes: Section numbers are Migne/Delarue's. At 3.6.3 Migne prints, between Rufinus's sentences, a Greek fragment taken from the end of Justinian's Letter to Menas and, beside it, Delarue's own Latin rendering of that Greek: ‘Λεγομένου τοῦ Θεοῦ πάντα γενέσθαι ἐν πᾶσιν, ὥσπερ οὐ δυνάμεθα κακίαν καταλιπεῖν, οὔτε Θεὸς πάντα γίνεται ἐν πᾶσιν, οὐδὲ ἄλογα ζῶα, ἵνα μὴ καὶ ἐν κακίᾳ ὁ Θεὸς γίνηται, καὶ ἐν ἀλόγοις ζώοις· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ ἄψυχα … Οὕτως οὐδὲ σώματα, ἅτινα τῇ ἰδίᾳ φύσει ἄψυχά ἐστιν.’ Roughly: when it is said that God will become all in all, God does not become all in all irrational animals, lest God also come to be in wickedness, nor in inanimate things, nor in bodies, which by their own nature are inanimate. The first clause is obscure in the scan and in Delarue's rendering and I would not rest an argument on my reading of it. (OCR slips fixed: ὲν to ἐν, ἇψυχα to ἄψυχα.) This Greek says something Rufinus's Latin does not say, which is the editions problem in miniature (see the next entry on 1.2.13). Delarue's note 44 records that the words ‘quod non solum in omnibus esse dicitur Deus, sed etiam omnia in omnibus’ were missing from earlier printed editions and supplied from the manuscripts. Note 57: ‘quod etiam finis’ (manuscripts) against ‘quae etiam finis’ (editions). Note 52: earlier editions added ‘id est diabolus’ after ‘inimicus’, an explicit gloss identifying the last enemy with the devil that the manuscripts do not have.

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), pp. 196-199 (citing 3.6.3) and n. 15
readings.position: Reads 3.6 as saying evil is abolished, not substance: apokatastasis is the return of all rational creatures and the dissolving of every contrast between good and evil (‘there will no longer be any contrast of good and evil, since evil nowhere exists’, p. 197), and he thinks the devil's redemption follows from Origen's ontology. For a detailed treatment he sends readers to Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (2013), pp. 144-156, without saying whether he agrees.
readings.side: reads 3.6 as teaching restoration of all rational creatures, evil ending because it has no being

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 25 and fn. 58
readings.position: Reads 3.6 as saying restoration comes through ‘word, reason, and doctrine’, not coercion, so free will is kept; cites MacDonald and Ramelli on how this avoids absolute determinism.
readings.side: reads 3.6 as universal restoration that respects freedom

readings.scholar: Jean Danielou (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), pp. 20-21, citing Danielou (1955, p. 289)
readings.position: Danielou sees two theses in Origen that pull apart, ‘the metaphysical necessity of the ultimate elimination of evil’ and the freedom of the creature, and asks how the re-establishment can be reconciled with freedom, concluding that Origen's attempts leave ‘a certain incoherence’. The report is about Origen's system, not 3.6 alone.
readings.side: doubts that the strict argument for the end of evil fits the stress on freedom

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Brill, 2013), cited in Sytsma, pp. 32 and n. 84
readings.position: Grounds the end of evil in its non-subsistence: ‘when it is chosen no longer by anyone,’ evil ‘will vanish according to its ontological non-subsistence’, and providence ‘does not force rational creatures' free will, but it acts in harmony with it’. Sytsma notes she does not explain why this must hold. The quotation is her general argument, which she applies to the 1.6.3 and 3.6 material.
readings.side: reads the end of evil as the natural result of free choices, so restoration is universal and free

passages.title: Where Rufinus and Justinian's Greek disagree: the Son as ‘image of God's goodness’ (On First Principles 1.2.13)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, On First Principles 1.2.13: Rufinus's Latin, and a Greek fragment preserved at the end of Justinian's Letter to Menas (543; Patrologia Graeca 86.1, Mansi 9)
passages.date: Origen's Greek before c. 230; Rufinus 397-98; Justinian 543
passages.original: RUFINUS: (1.2.13) Superest quid sit imago bonitatis ejus inquirere: in quo eadem, ut opinor, intelligi convenit quae superius de imagine ea quae per speculum deformatur, expressimus. Principalis namque bonitas sine dubio, ex qua Filius natus; qui per omnia imago est Patris, procul dubio etiam boni[…] … ne altera bonitas quam ea quae in Patre est, videatur in Filio. Neque aliqua dissimilitudo aut distantia bonitatis in Filio est. || JUSTINIAN (Greek, as printed in PG 11): Οὕτω τοίνυν ἡγοῦμαι· καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος καλῶς ἂν λεχθήσεσθαι ὅτι εἰκὼν ἀγαθότητος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν· καὶ τάχα καὶ Υἱὸς ἀγαθός, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ ὡς … [the rest of the sentence is lost in the scan]
passages.edition: Latin: P. Koetschau, GCS 22 (Leipzig, 1913), 1.2.13, page not confirmed. Greek: Justinian, Letter to Menas, Mansi 9 and PG 86.1 (neither opened); Koetschau prints it among his Greek fragments. Editions compared by Martens: Koetschau (1913); H. Gorgemanns and H. Karpp, Origenes: Vier Bucher von den Prinzipien (Darmstadt, 1976); Crouzel-Simonetti, SC 252 (1978); Behr, OECT (2017).
passages.checked_against: Both texts as printed in Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, cols. 143-144 and note 56 (Delarue's text), from the Fabio3rs/BibliothecaPatristica OCR transcription (teste/PG011, second batch, page 076), checked against the OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-11 scans (hvd page 077, mdp 085, njp 081). The three-column page runs Latin and Greek together, so the Latin is quoted only where contiguous, with […] at the gaps, and the Greek breaks off where the scan does. Greek OCR slips fixed: ἡγομαι to ἡγοῦμαι, ν to ἂν, εκὼν to εἰκὼν. The Greek was NOT checked against Justinian's letter itself.
passages.english: RUFINUS: It remains to ask what the image of his goodness is; in this, I think, the same must be understood as we set out above about the image formed in a mirror. For the primary goodness is, without doubt, that from which the Son is born, who in everything is the image of the Father, and so without doubt also the image of goodness … so that no other goodness than the one that is in the Father may seem to be in the Son. There is no unlikeness or distance of goodness in the Son. || JUSTINIAN'S GREEK: So, then, I think that of the Saviour too it would rightly be said that he is an image of God's goodness, but not goodness itself; and perhaps also that the Son is good, but not as … [Martens's English for the rest, from his reading of the Greek: the Son ‘is not purely and simply good’.]
passages.english_source: Own translation of the Latin and of the Greek as far as the scan reaches. The English in the last bracket is Peter Martens's gloss (JECS 2020, p. 320) and is not a translation of text I could read. Standard translations: Butterworth (1936), Behr (2017), neither opened. Contested rendering: ‘ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν’ (not goodness itself) against Rufinus's ‘no other goodness’: the first makes the Son's goodness derived and lesser, the second says it is the Father's goodness.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the clearest small case of the editions problem, and Peter Martens uses it for that purpose. If the Greek is Origen's, Rufinus has made the Son's goodness equal to the Father's; if Rufinus is right, Justinian's quotation is doctored or taken out of context. It is not about universal salvation itself, but every dispute over what Origen taught on the end turns on the same prior question: trust Rufinus's Latin, or the hostile Greek? The same fork appears at 3.6.3 (the Greek fragment on God ‘all in all’ above).
passages.textual_notes: Delarue (note 56 in PG 11) printed the Greek in brackets inside Rufinus's Latin and wrote that Justinian gives it at the end of his Letter to Menas, that he thinks it stood in the Greek text at this place, and that ‘it is clear how unreliable the faith of Rufinus is, who omitted it and substituted other things’. Jerome had already complained (Letter to Avitus) that Origen here ‘calls God the Father omnipotent, good and of perfect goodness; the Son not good, but a breath and an image of goodness’. Note 57 gives the manuscript reading of Rufinus: ‘ne altera bonitas quam ea quae in Patre est, videatur in Filio’ (earlier editions: ‘exsistit in Filium praeter eam quae est a Patre’). Martens (p. 321 n. 43) reports that Koetschau supports the Greek by a parallel at Commentary on Matthew 15.10, where Origen uses the same biblical texts (Wisdom 7:26; Colossians 1:15). Koetschau's own page and line not confirmed.

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader) and Charles Delarue (editor)
readings.work: Jerome, Letter to Avitus (Letter 124), as quoted in Delarue's note 56, PG 11 cols. 143-144; Delarue's edition of Origen (1733-59) as reprinted in PG 11
readings.position: Both take the Greek in Justinian's letter as what Origen wrote and Rufinus as having left it out. Delarue says so in as many words (‘how unreliable the faith of Rufinus is’); Jerome complains that Origen made the Son a mere image of goodness.
readings.side: trusts the hostile Greek and Jerome against Rufinus

readings.scholar: Paul Koetschau and Gorgemanns-Karpp (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Martens, ‘The Modern Editions of Peri Archon’, Journal of Early Christian Studies 28.2 (2020), pp. 303-331, esp. 315-316, 320-321 and n. 43
readings.position: In Martens's grouping these editors print a ‘mosaic’ text that uses other witnesses to correct Rufinus. At 1.2.13 each ‘regards Justinian's fragment as genuine and Rufinus's corresponding translation as corrupt’; Koetschau supports it from Commentary on Matthew 15.10. Martens says Koetschau ‘interrupts the progression of Rufinus's translation’ so often that readers may mistake the other sources for Rufinus's text.
readings.side: trusts the Greek fragment and builds the Latin text around it

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel and Manlio Simonetti (as reported by Peter Martens)
readings.work: Martens, JECS 28.2 (2020), pp. 314, 321 n. 43; Crouzel's commentary volume to SC 252-253 (1978)
readings.position: Their main edition prints Rufinus's text (Koetschau's text with only minor changes) and puts the other witnesses in the commentary volumes. On this passage Crouzel's commentary calls Justinian's report ‘perhaps authentic’ and suggests Rufinus may have shortened it for Latin readers, which is a milder charge than Koetschau's.
readings.side: prints Rufinus; allows the Greek may be authentic and Rufinus abridged

readings.scholar: John Behr
readings.work: Origen: On First Principles, Oxford Early Christian Texts (OUP, 2017), as reported in Martens, JECS 28.2 (2020), pp. 313-315, 328, and in John Cavadini's Foreword to the Christian Classics edition of Butterworth (2013), pp. vii-viii
readings.position: Behr edits Rufinus's Latin and puts Koetschau's other fragments in an ‘Appendix II: Koetschau's Fragments’; Martens does not say what Behr makes of 1.2.13 itself. Cavadini, writing of the new approach, says the text of Rufinus ‘stands alone’ except where the Philocalia gives a long Greek witness.
readings.side: prints Rufinus alone and keeps the Greek separate

readings.scholar: G. W. Butterworth, as characterised by John Cavadini and Daniel Heide
readings.work: Cavadini, Foreword to Origen: On First Principles (Christian Classics/Ave Maria Press, 2013 reprint of Butterworth), pp. vii-viii; Heide, Arc 44 (2016), pp. 50, 57-61
readings.position: Butterworth (1936) translated Koetschau's text and ‘divided the page between Latin and Greek columns’; Cavadini says he ‘fully adopted, and even extended’ Koetschau's suspicion of Rufinus, using sources ‘as hostile as the anathemata of Justinian’ as if they were neutral. Heide agrees and adds that Crouzel-Simonetti are ‘an important corrective to Koetschau’. Neither report speaks of 1.2.13 specifically, and I did not open Butterworth.
readings.side: critics of the Koetschau-Butterworth method, who trust Rufinus more

passages.title: Why the full teaching on punishment is not for the many (Against Celsus 6.26)
passages.original: Ὅσα δ᾿ εἰς τὸν τόπον λεχθείη ἂν, οὔτε πᾶσιν οὔτε τοῦ παρόντος καιροῦ ἐστι διηγήσασθαι· ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἀκίνδυνον τὴν τῶν τοιούτων σαφήνειαν πιστεῦσαι γραφῇ. ἅτε τῶν πολλῶν οὐ χρῃζόντων πλείονος διδασκαλίας παρὰ τὴν περὶ τῆς κατὰ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων κολάσεως. εἰς γὰρ τὰ ὑπερέκεινα αὐτῆς οὐ χρήσιμον ἀναβαίνειν διὰ τοὺς μόγις φόβῳ τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως κἂν συστέλλοντας ἐπὶ ποσὸν τῆς κακίας καὶ τῶν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἁμαρτανομένων χύσιν.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke 2: Buch V-VIII gegen Kelsos, GCS 3 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1899), p. 96 (the page marker in the digital transcription; line numbers not given). Modern translation: H. Chadwick, Contra Celsum (Cambridge, 1953), not opened. Public-domain English: ANF 4 (Crombie), not opened.
passages.checked_against: Perseus Digital Library TEI transcription of Koetschau (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg001.perseus-grc1), which carries Koetschau's page numbers. One obvious typing slip fixed: πολῶν to πολλῶν. This is an electronic transcription of the edition, not the printed page.
passages.english: As for what might be said on this subject, it is neither for everyone nor for the present occasion to set it out; and it is not free of danger to entrust the plain statement of such matters to writing, since the many need no more teaching than the one about the punishment of sinners. To go beyond it is not useful, because of those who, barely, through fear of eternal punishment, hold back to some extent the outpouring of evil and of the sins that come from it.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Contested rendering: ‘αἰωνίου κολάσεως’ (eternal punishment; or age-long, lasting for an age, the meaning argued by Ramelli and Konstan for aionios, see the Romans 6.5 entry). Note that Origen himself uses the word here in the phrase the many fear, and does not say whether he thinks it is the right word. ‘τὸν τόπον’ (this subject, this place): the lines before it speak of purification by fire in Jerusalem, so the subject is the fire of punishment.
passages.why_it_matters: This is the passage most often cited for the claim that Origen held a fuller doctrine than he taught the simple. He says the plain account of punishment is enough for the many and that going beyond it would not help those who are held back from evil by fear of an ‘eternal’ punishment. He does not say what lies beyond it, and he does not call the doctrine of eternal punishment false.
passages.textual_notes: The extract begins mid-argument; the previous sentence in 6.26 (not quoted) speaks of punishments ‘in connection with Jerusalem’, of souls being melted down, and of Zechariah's ‘talent of lead’. No variant of consequence is recorded in the transcription. Chapter division is Koetschau's.

readings.scholar: Pierre Batiffol
readings.work: ‘Apocatastasis’, Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (1907), s.v.; the copy read is on catholic.com
readings.position: Says Origen ‘does not seem to have regarded the doctrine of the apokatastasis as one meant to be preached to all’, citing Against Celsus 6.26. In the same article he cites On First Principles 1.6.3 (Origen ‘does not venture to assert’ that all evil angels will return) and the Commentary on Romans for the view that Origen was cautious and at times inconsistent, and he relies on Tixeront.
readings.side: reads Origen as teaching apokatastasis as a rule, but cautiously and not publicly

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide
readings.work: ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), p. 197 n. 13
readings.position: Takes 6.26 (‘It is not right to explain to everybody all that might be said on this subject’, in the English he uses) to show that the devil's ultimate fate is one of the things Origen thought unsuitable to explain to everyone, though the logic of his ontology seems to require the devil's restoration.
readings.side: reads the reticence as hiding a universalist conclusion

readings.scholar: Tom Greggs (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 27; Greggs's own work was not identified in the report
readings.position: Argues, in Hannen's report, that Origen's universalism varies by genre and audience. Hannen himself puts down Origen's passages that seem to support separation after death (Against Celsus 3.16, 3.31) to pastoral concerns.
readings.side: reads Origen's wording as adjusted to his audience, not as inconsistency

passages.title: The Word will master every rational soul, and evil will be abolished (Against Celsus 8.72)
passages.original: ἡμεῖς δὲ τῆς λογικῆς φύσεώς φαμεν ὅλης κρατῆσαί ποτε τὸν λόγον καὶ μεταποιῆσαι πᾶσαν ψυχὴν εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ τελειότητα, ἐπὰν [289] ἕκαστος ψιλῇ χρησάμενος τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ἕληται ἃ βούλεται καὶ γένηται ἐν οἷς εἵλατο· καὶ φαμεν ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν εἰκὸς, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν (ἐν) τοῖς σώμασι νοσημάτων καὶ τραυμάτων τινὰ τῶν συμβαινόντων ἰσχυρότερα εἶναι πάσης ἰατρικῆς τέχνης, οὕτως ἐπὶ τῶν ψυχῶν εἶναί τι τῶν ἀπὸ κακίας ἀδύνατον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι λογικοῦ καὶ θεοῦ θεραπευθῆναι. πάντων γὰρ τῶν ἐν ψυχῇ κακῶν δυνατώτερος ὢν ὁ λόγος καὶ ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ θεραπεία προσάγει κατὰ βούλησιν θεοῦ ἑκάστῳ αὐτὴν, καὶ τὸ τέλος τῶν πραγμάτων ἀναιρεθῆναί ἐστι τὴν κακίαν· πότερον δὲ ὥστε μηδαμῇ μηδαμῶς ἔτι αὐτὴν ἐπιτραπῆναι δύνασθαι ἢ μὴ, οὐ τοῦ παρόντος ἐστὶ λόγου διδάξαι.
passages.edition: P. Koetschau, Origenes Werke 2, GCS 3 (Leipzig, 1899), pp. 288-289 (the bracketed [289] marks Koetschau's page break; (ἐν) is Koetschau's supplement). Chadwick (1953) and ANF 4 not opened.
passages.checked_against: Perseus TEI transcription of Koetschau (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg001.perseus-grc1) with his page numbers. Two stray page markers from the digital file (not Koetschau's) were removed, one of which fell in the middle of the word αὐτήν. The transcription is electronic, not the printed page.
passages.english: But we say that the Word will one day master the whole rational nature and remake every soul into his own perfection, when each, using only his own freedom, chooses what he wishes and becomes what he has chosen. And we say that, as with diseases and wounds of bodies some are stronger than every medical art, it is not likely that among souls anything arising from evil is incurable by the Word, who is over all, and by God. For the Word, being more powerful than all the evils in the soul, and the healing that is in him, brings it to each according to God's will; and the end of things is that evil is abolished. Whether so that it can in no way ever again be allowed to arise, or not, is not for the present discussion to teach.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard comparisons: Chadwick (1953); ANF 4 (public domain, Crombie); neither opened. Contested renderings: ‘κρατῆσαι’ (master, prevail over, gain control of); ‘μεταποιῆσαι’ (remake or transform); ‘ἀναιρεθῆναι τὴν κακίαν’ (that evil be abolished, taken away, destroyed); ‘ἐπιτραπῆναι’ in the last clause (be allowed, be given leave, be turned over: the sentence leaves open whether evil could ever be readmitted).
passages.why_it_matters: This is Origen's most direct statement in a work he wrote for publication, late in life, that the aim of the Word's healing is to abolish evil in every rational soul. He says it as what ‘we’ say, not as a guess. Then he refuses to decide, in this discussion, whether evil could ever return. Readers divide over how much weight the first half carries and how much the refusal carries.
passages.textual_notes: The task text for this entry spoke of a ‘perhaps’ in the passage; there is no ‘perhaps’ (τάχα) in these lines of Koetschau's Greek. The hedge is the closing sentence, which explicitly sets aside the question whether evil can be so abolished that it can never again be admitted. The next sentences (not quoted) bring in Zephaniah 3:7-11 as prophetic support. Against Celsus survives in Greek in the Tura papyrus for books 1-2 and in the manuscript tradition for the rest, so Rufinus's problem does not arise here.

readings.scholar: Chris Hannen
readings.work: ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, Stimulus 23.2 (year not confirmed), p. 27
readings.position: Reads 8.72 as saying each soul freely chooses what the Word wills and ‘the end of the treatment is the abolition of evil’, and so as pointing to universal restoration; he adds that other passages (Against Celsus 3.16, 3.31) seem to support separation after death, which he puts down to pastoral concerns.
readings.side: reads 8.72 as a statement of universal restoration

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, p. 27, citing Crouzel
readings.position: ‘The best we can ascertain is that Origen hoped for universal salvation’, and no clear universalist reading is possible. This is Crouzel's general position, in Hannen's report, not a comment on 8.72 by number.
readings.side: reads Origen as hoping for, not asserting, universal salvation

readings.scholar: Joseph Heine and Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Chris Hannen)
readings.work: Hannen, ‘Rob Bell and Origen’, pp. 27-28 (Heine's work not named in the report); Ramelli's reply at p. 28
readings.position: Heine suggests that Origen reconsidered limits on redemption in later life, which he calls ‘a defendable, but not an unquestionable, conclusion’. Against Celsus is a late work (c. 248), so this bears on how to read 8.72. Ramelli disagrees and holds that Origen did not change his mind.
readings.side: Heine: late hedging on the end; Ramelli: continuity

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Steven Nemes)
readings.work: Nemes, review of Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis, Journal of Analytic Theology 3 (2015), pp. 227-233, reporting Ramelli (Brill, 2013), p. 193
readings.position: Ramelli's book argues that ‘No being is incurable for the Christ-Logos’ and that apokatastasis is professed in all of Origen's works (p. 208). Nemes does not link the first sentence to 8.72 by number; it matches the argument of 8.72 and is placed here for that reason.
readings.side: reads Origen as consistently teaching that the Logos can heal every being

passages.title: ‘You deceived me, Lord’: the physician, the father and the hidden mystery (Homilies on Jeremiah 20.3-4)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Homilies on Jeremiah, Homily 20, sections 3-4 (on Jeremiah 20:7)
passages.original: (20.3, p. 181) τὸ κατὰ τὸν τόπον μυστήριον κεκρύφθαι δεῖ, ἵνα μὴ ἐκκακήσῃ ὁ πολύς, ἵνα μὴ μαθὼν τὰ πράγματα προσδοκήσῃ τὴν ἔξοδον οὐχ ὡς ἀνάπαυσιν, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς κόλασιν. (20.3, p. 182) ἄλλη γὰρ ἡ ἀπάτη ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἄλλη ἡ ἀπάτη ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως. (20.4, p. 183) πόσοι δὲ νομιζόμενοι σοφοί, εὑρόντες τὸ περὶ κολάσεως ἀληθὲς καὶ διελθόντες δῆθεν τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης, ἐν χείρονι γεγόνασι βίῳ; ἐλυσιτέλει αὐτοὺς φρονεῖν, ὡς ἐφρόνουν πρότερον περὶ τοῦ ‘ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτήσει’ καὶ ὅτι ‘τὸ πῦρ αὐτῶν οὐ σβεσθήσεται’
passages.edition: E. Klostermann, Origenes Werke 3: Jeremiahomilien, Klageliederkommentar, Erklarung der Samuelbucher, GCS 6 (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1901), Homily 20.3-4, pp. 179-184 (the quoted lines fall on pp. 181, 182 and 183 by the page markers in the digital file). A second edition by P. Nautin appeared in 1983, and P. Nautin and P. Husson edited the Greek with French translation in SC 238 (1977); I did not check either. English: J. C. Smith, Fathers of the Church 97 (1998), not opened.
passages.checked_against: TEI transcription of Klostermann (First1KGreek, tlg2042.tlg021.opp-grc1), which keeps Klostermann's page numbers and his editorial marks. One obvious typing slip fixed: πρότρον to πρότερον. Electronic transcription, not the printed page.
passages.english: (20.3) The mystery in this passage has to be kept hidden, so that the many may not lose heart, so that, learning how things are, they may not expect their departure as a rest but as a punishment. (20.3) For the deception from God is one thing, the deception from the serpent another. (20.4) How many who are thought wise, having found the truth about punishment and gone through, as they suppose, the business of the deception, have fallen into a worse way of life? It would have profited them to go on thinking as they used to think about ‘their worm shall not die’ and ‘their fire shall not be quenched’.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Contested renderings: ‘ἀπάτη’ and the verb of Jeremiah 20:7 (the Septuagint's ἠπάτησάς με: deceived, tricked; the Hebrew verb is commonly rendered ‘enticed’ or ‘persuaded’, which fits Origen's argument that the deception is for the person's good); ‘δῆθεν’ (supposedly, as they think); ‘τὸ περὶ κολάσεως ἀληθές’ (the truth about punishment: Origen does not say what he thinks it is).
passages.why_it_matters: With Against Celsus 6.26 this is where Origen most openly says that what the many are told about punishment may differ from what the wise are told. The disputed point is what the ‘truth about punishment’ is. Read closely, 20.3 says the hidden thing is that the baptised too must pass through punishment (the preceding lines say every sinner must be punished, and that his own ‘wood’ must be burned in him), not that all will be saved; 20.4 says some who found the truth took it for permission and did worse. The lines read do not say the truth is that punishment ends, though that is how the passage is often read.
passages.textual_notes: Klostermann's text has a gap in 20.3 (‘. . .’) after ‘καὶ τὸν σοφώτατον’, where the manuscript is defective or the editor sees a lacuna; the sentence just before the quoted lines is broken for the same reason. Another clause early in 20.3 reads ‘οὖν ἄλλως δυνάμενον’ in the transcription, which may be a slip for ‘οὐκ ἄλλως’; it is not quoted. The Greek homilies were preserved in a few manuscripts; Jerome's Latin translation covers other homilies (14 in all), not Homily 20.

passages.title: Love never fails: can restored beings fall again? (Commentary on Romans 5.10)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans 5.10 (on Romans 6:9-10), Rufinus's abridged Latin translation; Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1053-1054
passages.date: Origen's Greek c. 244 (dating uncertain); Rufinus's Latin c. 405-407
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's abridged translation; no Greek survives for this part)
passages.original: … potest fieri ut in quocunque statu fuerit anima, et in quacunque perfectione virtutum, quoniam virtus mutabilis est, lapsum possit incurrere … Haec ergo et his similia proponentes, easdem etiam in futuris saeculis dispensationes a Christo repetendas esse arbitrantur. Sed ad haec nos breviter prout possumus respondebimus. Manere quidem naturae rationabili semper liberum arbitrium non negamus; sed tantam esse vim crucis Christi, et mortis hujus, quam in saeculorum fine suscepit, asserimus, quae ad sanitatem et remedium non solum praesentis et futuri, sed etiam praeteritorum saeculorum, et non solum humano huic nostro ordini, sed etiam caelestibus virtutibus ordinibusque sufficiat. … Quid autem sit quod in futuris saeculis teneat arbitrii libertatem, ne rursum corruat in peccatum, brevi nos sermone Apostolus docet, dicens: ‘Charitas nunquam cadit.’ Idcirco enim et fide et spe major charitas dicitur, quia sola erit per quam delinqui ultra non poterit. … Et ideo merito charitas quae sola omnium major est, omnem creaturam continebit a lapsu. Tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus.
passages.edition: C. P. Hammond Bammel, Der Romerbrief-Kommentar des Origenes: kritische Ausgabe der Ubersetzung Rufins, Vetus Latina: Aus der Geschichte der lateinischen Bibel 16, 33, 34 (Freiburg: Herder, 1990, 1997, 1998); Book 5 should be in the second volume, 33; not opened, page not confirmed. English: T. P. Scheck, Origen: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, Fathers of the Church 103 (2001), where a web post puts Book 5.10 at p. 376; not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Hammond Bammel. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1053-1054 (Delarue's text), from the OCR page transcription OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-14 (nyp.33433081862280_ocr, page 538). The page has two columns read line by line; the quoted sentences were put back in order and the lemma lines of the right-hand column (the Romans text being commented on) left out. ‘Charitas nunquam cadit’ is from 1 Corinthians 13:8. Spelling and ligatures normalised (c/ch left as printed). The chapter number 5.10 comes from the request, not from the scan.
passages.english: … it can happen that in whatever state the soul has been, and in whatever perfection of virtues, since virtue can change, it may incur a fall … [Those] who put forward these and similar arguments think that the same dispensations must be repeated by Christ in future ages. But to these we shall reply briefly, as well as we can. We do not deny that free choice remains with rational nature always; but we declare that the power of Christ's cross, and of this death which he took upon himself at the end of the ages, is enough for the healing and remedy not only of the present and the future, but also of the past ages, and not only of this human order of ours but also of the heavenly powers and orders. … What it is that preserves freedom of choice in the ages to come, so that it does not fall back into sin, the Apostle teaches us in a few words, saying: ‘Love never falls.’ For that is why love is called greater than faith and hope: because it alone will be the means by which there can be no more sinning. … And so, rightly, love, which alone is greater than all, will keep the whole creation from falling. Then God will be all in all.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard English: Scheck (FC 103, 2001), not opened. Contested renderings: ‘saeculum’ (age, world or epoch); ‘charitas’ (love or charity); ‘creaturam continebit a lapsu’ (will hold the whole creation back from falling); ‘liberum arbitrium’ (free choice or free will).
passages.why_it_matters: This is Origen's answer, as Rufinus gives it, to the objection that a creature with free choice could fall again even after being restored, so that the saving work would have to be repeated in each future age. Jerome claimed Origen's system ended in endless cycles of rise and fall (Letter 124); this passage says the opposite, that love will secure the creation, and so is cited against Jerome. It also does not say that every being is already restored.
passages.textual_notes: Rufinus says in his preface that he shortened the Commentary on Romans, which Eusebius counted as fifteen books, to ten (this is the usual account; Sytsma cites the preface only for the abridgment). The small Greek papyrus finds from Tura cover only Romans 3:5-5:7 in this commentary (Scherer 1957, usual reference, unchecked), so there is no Greek control at 5.10. The PG apparatus: note 51, ‘nec’ would suit the sense better than ‘ne rursum corruat’, but all manuscripts and editions read ‘ne’; note 53, the final clause ‘Tunc erit Deus omnia in omnibus’ is preceded in earlier editions and one manuscript by different wording (‘maxima est … tunc cum erit Deus’ and ‘mater est … cum erit Deus’). The lemma it comments on is Romans 6:10 (‘the life he lives, he lives to God’).

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Aidan Kimel)
readings.work: Kimel, ‘An Open Letter to Dr Cyril Jenkins’ (2024), n. 10, citing Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (Brill, 2013), pp. 137-215
readings.position: Kimel quotes, without a location, a passage of the Commentary on Romans on ‘the power and effectiveness of Christ's cross and of his death’ saving ‘all the past’ ages, which matches this chapter. The reading he draws, with Ramelli, is that the rational nature keeps its free will while the cross is powerful enough to save across the ages. I matched the passage to 5.10 myself.
readings.side: reads the passage as compatible with free will and a universal salvation across the ages

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), p. 25, citing Crouzel (1985, pp. 264-65)
readings.position: ‘Certainty about a universal apocatastasis would be in contradiction to the authenticity of the free will’; a universal apocatastasis could only be ‘a great hope’. This states the problem 5.10 is written to answer, but the report does not discuss 5.10 itself.
readings.side: holds that freedom rules out certainty of universal salvation

readings.scholar: Jerome (ancient reader)
readings.work: Letter 124 to Avitus, 124.3.6 (Hilberg, CSEL 56, p. 99), Latin as given in this survey's c400 file
readings.position: Charges that Origen's system means rational creatures change places ‘not once and suddenly but repeatedly’: we shall be angels, and, if we act carelessly, demons; and demons, if they lay hold of virtue, will reach angelic dignity. If Rufinus's Romans commentary is Origen's own, 5.10 contradicts that charge.
readings.side: ancient hostile reader: reads Origen's system as allowing endless falls

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Lee Sytsma)
readings.work: Sytsma, dissertation, p. 32, citing Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis (2013), p. 113 and n. 84
readings.position: ‘Providence does not force rational creatures' free will, but it acts in harmony with it’, and once souls know the Good ‘all will voluntarily adhere to the Good’. Sytsma remarks that she does not explain why this must hold. Again the report is about the problem, not 5.10.
readings.side: holds that providence and freedom agree, so restoration is secure and free

passages.title: What ‘eternal’ means: a lifetime, an age, or without end (Commentary on Romans 6.5)
passages.author_work_ref: Origen, Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans 6.5 (on Romans 6:22-23), Rufinus's abridged Latin translation; Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1067-1068
passages.date: Origen's Greek c. 244 (dating uncertain); Rufinus's Latin c. 405-407
passages.language: Latin (Rufinus's abridged translation; Greek not preserved here)
passages.original: … et erit tibi servus in aeternum. Aeternum hic sine dubio tempus vitae hominis posuit. Et iterum in Ecclesiaste dicitur: ‘Generatio vadit, et generatio venit, terra autem in aeternum stat’: hic aeternum praesentis saeculi tempus ostendit. Ubi vero dicit ‘vitam aeternam,’ ad illud aspiciendum est quod ipse Salvator dixit: ‘Haec est autem vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum …’ … Sicut ergo semper cum Domino esse, finem non habet, ita et vita aeterna nullum finem habere credenda est. … Ego non puto etiam hoc vacuum esse, quod ad vitam aeternam addidit ‘in Christo Jesu Domino nostro’; sed quia fortassis sciri voluit aliud esse vitam aeternam solum, et aliud vitam aeternam in Christo Jesu.
passages.edition: C. P. Hammond Bammel, Vetus Latina: Aus der Geschichte der lateinischen Bibel 33 or 34 (Freiburg: Herder, 1997/1998); not opened, page not confirmed. English: T. P. Scheck, Fathers of the Church 104 (2002); Heide cites this passage as ‘VI.5.9’ (the section number is his). Not opened.
passages.checked_against: NOT Hammond Bammel. Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, cols. 1067-1068 (Delarue's text), from the OCR page transcription OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev/Vol.-14 (nyp.33433081862280_ocr, page 545). The scan reads the two columns line by line; the quoted sentences were put back in order. I left out one sentence, ‘Et illi enim qui surgent in confusionem et opprobrium sempiternum, habebunt quidem vitam aeternam, non tamen in Christo Jesu, sed in confusione et opprobrio aeterno …’, because the OCR of it is doubtful; if it reads as it appears, it applies ‘aeternam’ both to life and to shame and should be checked in the critical edition. The chapter number 6.5 comes from the request, not from the scan.
passages.english: … and he will be your servant for ever [aeternum]. Here ‘for ever’ undoubtedly stands for the time of a man's life. And again, in Ecclesiastes it is said: ‘A generation goes and a generation comes, but the earth stands for ever’; here ‘for ever’ shows the time of the present age. But where he says ‘eternal life’, we must look to what the Saviour himself said: ‘This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God …’ … As, therefore, being always with the Lord has no end, so eternal life too must be believed to have no end. … I do not think even this is empty, that to ‘eternal life’ he added ‘in Christ Jesus our Lord’; perhaps he wanted it known that eternal life alone is one thing, and eternal life in Christ Jesus another.
passages.english_source: Own translation. Standard English: Scheck (FC 104, 2002), not opened. The key word is Latin ‘aeternum’, rendering Greek aionios (aion: an age; aionios: of the age, age-long, or, in later usage, eternal). Contested renderings: ‘in aeternum’ (for ever, for an age, for a lifetime); ‘vita aeterna’ (eternal life, or life of the age to come).
passages.why_it_matters: This is the passage scholars cite when they argue that Origen himself knew ‘eternal’ can mean a stretch of time. He gives two examples where it means a lifetime or the present age, then says that eternal life with the Lord has no end. So it supports both readings: ‘eternal’ need not mean endless, and Origen holds that eternal life does. Which weight it carries in the dispute over eternal punishment depends on whether the same word is allowed to shift between life and punishment.
passages.textual_notes: Rufinus's abridgment and the lack of Greek mean the Latin ‘aeternum’ could stand for aionios or for another Greek word. The PG apparatus (note 28) has variants for ‘surgunt/surgent’ and ‘habent/habebunt’ in the next sentence, and the editions of 1500s and 1600s omit some of the words in the preceding sentence about ‘fructum’ (note 26). The OCR is poor at several points in the right-hand column (garbled Greek ‘Jesu’ as ‘ἔθευ’, now corrected by sense).

readings.scholar: Daniel Heide (relying on Ilaria Ramelli and David Konstan)
readings.work: Heide, ‘Apokatastasis: The Resolution of Good and Evil in Origen and Eriugena’, Dionysius 33 (2015), pp. 202-203 and nn. 20, 28; Ramelli and Konstan, Terms for Eternity (2007)
readings.position: Takes Origen to use aion in the sense of an age or epoch, not eternity, so that scriptural ‘eternal’ punishment may be finite; Heide notes that the interpretation of Ramelli is ‘controversial’ (p. 202) and that Eriugena did not take this route.
readings.side: reads Origen's ‘eternal’ as age-long, so punishment can end

readings.scholar: Henri Crouzel (as cited by Daniel Heide)
readings.work: Crouzel, ‘L'Hades et la Geheenne selon Origene’ (1978), cited in Heide, Dionysius 33 (2015), n. 28
readings.position: Cited by Heide for Origen's ambiguity on how long punishment lasts; Heide's text gives no Crouzel wording.
readings.side: reads Origen on the duration of punishment as ambiguous

readings.scholar: Michael McClymond
readings.work: ‘Origenes Vindicatus vel Rufinus Redivivus’, Theological Studies 76.4 (2015), p. 824 n. 23
readings.position: Discusses Ramelli's argument that aionios need not mean ‘eternal’ in an absolute sense and calls it partly meritorious; the part I saw does not analyse Origen's own usage or say where the argument falls short.
readings.side: accepts part of the age-long argument but not its use as a proof of Origen's universalism

readings.scholar: Ilaria Ramelli (as reported by Steven Nemes)
readings.work: Nemes, review of Ramelli, The Christian Doctrine of Apokatastasis, Journal of Analytic Theology 3 (2015), pp. 227-233, reporting Ramelli (2013) p. 160
readings.position: Ramelli cites Origen's phrase ‘life after aionios life’ as evidence that aionios does not mean ‘eternal’. Nemes does not tie the phrase to the Romans commentary by number.
readings.side: reads aionios in Origen as age-long, not endless

other_findings.claim: Peter Martens divides the modern editors of Peri Archon into two groups: those who print mainly Rufinus's translation (Merlin, Crouzel and Simonetti, Behr) and those who print a ‘mosaic’ text drawing on other witnesses (Delarue, Koetschau, Gorgemanns and Karpp, Rius-Camps, Fernandez). Koetschau built on Delarue; Crouzel-Simonetti print Koetschau's Rufinus text with only minor changes.
other_findings.source: Martens, ‘The Modern Editions of Peri Archon’, Journal of Early Christian Studies 28.2 (2020), pp. 303-331, esp. 313-316, as read through a fetch tool (https://www.academia.edu/43470693/T); the last 7,000 characters were not read

other_findings.claim: Koetschau's 1913 text is the basis for Butterworth's English translation (1936); Cavadini says Koetschau's presentation was ‘predicated on a hermeneutic of thoroughgoing suspicion regarding Rufinus's translation’ and that Butterworth adopted and extended it. Rufinus's Latin is ‘the only complete attestation of the text remaining from antiquity’.
other_findings.source: John Cavadini, Foreword to Origen: On First Principles (Christian Classics/Ave Maria Press, 2013), pp. vii-viii, from the publisher's excerpt PDF

other_findings.claim: Daniel Heide argues that Koetschau and Butterworth trust hostile witnesses (Justinian's letter, the 543 anathemas) over Rufinus, and that Jerome is treated too uncritically; Koetschau inserted anathemas II and VI of 543 into the text (p. 59). Heide calls Crouzel-Simonetti ‘an important corrective to Koetschau’.
other_findings.source: Heide, ‘Heresy, Hermeneutics, and the Hellenization of Christianity: A Reappraisal of Embodiment in Origen's De Principiis’, Arc 44 (2016), pp. 49-67, esp. 50, 56-61

other_findings.claim: Reviews and studies of the Behr edition to follow up: David Bentley Hart's review in the Journal of Orthodox Christian Studies 3.1 (2020), pp. 103-107, and Martens's article above (both listed in Wikipedia's article ‘On the First Principles’). Not read.

Pierre Batiffol reads the Commentary on Romans (cited as VIII, 9) as saying that Lucifer ‘will not be converted, even at the end of time’, and On First Principles 1.6.3 as showing Origen ‘does not venture to assert’ that all the evil angels will return to God. These are the main texts used by those who say Origen did not teach the devil's salvation. Neither passage is covered in this entry; Comm. Rom. 8.9 was not read.
other_findings.source: Batiffol, ‘Apocatastasis’, Catholic Encyclopedia vol. 1 (1907), as read on catholic.com

other_findings.claim: Ramelli, as reported by Sytsma, cites On First Principles 1.6.3 for the claim that Satan will be saved ‘not qua devil, arch-enemy, and death’ but as a creature of God (p. 32 n. 83, citing Ramelli 2013, p. 144 n. 83). The c400 file in this survey compares Jerome's Letter 124 with Rufinus at 1.6.3.
other_findings.source: Lee Sytsma, Reconciling Universal Salvation and Freedom of Choice in Origen of Alexandria (Marquette dissertation, 2018), p. 32 n. 83

other_findings.claim: Reading of the Greek, not of a scholar: in Homilies on Jeremiah 20.3 the ‘mystery’ the many must not hear is introduced by the claim that every sinner must be punished and that Origen's own ‘wood’ must be burned in him, so the hidden thing is that believers too will meet punishment after death. The passage never says what ‘the truth about punishment’ in 20.4 is.
other_findings.source: First1KGreek transcription of Klostermann, GCS 6 (1901), Hom. Jer. 20.3-4, read in full

other_findings.claim: In the Preface of On First Principles (section 5), eternal fire for sinners and eternal life for the saved are listed among the points ‘defined in the church's preaching’, alongside free will. A reader who takes this as Origen's own rule of faith will not read 1.6 or 3.6 as denying all punishment.
other_findings.source: Migne, Patrologia Graeca 11, col. 117-118, Preface 5, as quoted in the first passage

other_findings.claim: Reported by Wikipedia from standard works: Daley (The Hope of the Early Church, 1991, p. 58) holds Origen ‘strongly believed in the final salvation of all humans’; Crouzel (Origen, English trans. 1989, p. 285, cited as 1990) and Mark Scott (Journey Back to God, 2012) are cited for the view that it is doubtful Origen taught the doctrine; Norris (Westminster Handbook to Origen) says his positions ‘have often seemed contradictory’.
other_findings.source: Wikipedia, ‘Apokatastasis’, as read through a fetch tool (the originals were not opened)

problems: (1) Koetschau's critical text of On First Principles could not be read in sections: archive.org (origeneswerke05orig) was reachable only through a tool that returns about the first 59,000 characters, which stops inside the Introduction. All Latin of On First Principles and of the Romans commentary is therefore Migne's Patrologia Graeca 11 and 14 (Delarue's text) from OCR page images on GitHub, and every status V for those passages means 'checked against that printed edition', not against Koetschau, Hammond Bammel, Crouzel-Simonetti or Behr. Orthography and some readings may differ in Koetschau. (2) Large parts of some OCR pages were missing: On First Principles 3.6.5 (the destruction of the last enemy as the end of its hostile will, not its substance) was not obtained, nor the middle of Rufinus's Latin at 3.6.2-3 or 1.2.13; the Greek fragment of Justinian at 1.2.13 breaks off in the scan. Justinian's Letter to Menas itself (PG 86.1, Mansi 9) was not opened; the Greek is as Migne prints it in PG 11. (3) Butterworth, Behr, Crouzel-Simonetti, Hammond Bammel, Chadwick, Scheck and Smith were not opened; how Butterworth and Behr treat 1.2.13 specifically is not known beyond Martens, Cavadini and Heide's general descriptions. (4) No English public-domain translation (ANF) was read, so every English rendering is my own. (5) No named scholarly reading of Homilies on Jeremiah 20.3-4 could be found online, so that passage's readings list is empty rather than padded; the closest neighbours (Batiffol, Heide and Greggs on Against Celsus 6.26) are about a different text. (6) The readings for Commentary on Romans 5.10 are partly about the problem the passage answers (freedom and certainty), not about 5.10 by name, and say so; Kimel's note quoted the passage without a location, and I matched it. (7) Most scholars were read through a web fetch tool that returns summaries with short quotations (Martens, Heide, McClymond, Sytsma, Hannen, Nemes, Cavadini, Batiffol, Kimel), so their statuses are S, not V; McClymond and Sytsma were read only for the footnotes and passages the tool reported, and Sytsma's chapters on apocatastasis (pp. 134-180) were beyond the reachable text. Hannen's journal year and Greggs's and Heine's works were not identified. Ramelli, Edwards, Tzamalikos, Daley, Heine, Scott, Ludlow and Hart were not read directly; Crouzel and Daley page references come from Hannen, Sytsma or Wikipedia. (8) The Hilberg citation for Jerome's Letter 124 and the Koetschau pages for 1.6.2-3 are taken from the c400 file, not rechecked. (9) Contra Celsum 8.72 contains no ‘perhaps’ in the Greek read; the request's description of it was not borne out. (10) Perseus/First1K transcriptions of Koetschau and Klostermann were used for the Greek; they are electronic copies and a few typing slips may remain.
